document.title: Motion to Intervene and Comments of Talen Energy Corporation re PJM Governance and Stakeholder Reforms
document.group: PJM governance and stakeholder reform vote

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
 
 
PJM Governance and Stakeholder  
Reforms 
) 
) 
) 
) 
 
Docket No. AD26-7-000 
 
MOTION TO INTERVENE AND COMMENTS OF 
TALEN ENERGY CORPORATION 
The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC” or “Commission”) established 
independent system operators (“ISOs”) based on a set of principles, including that the 
“management and administration of the ISO should be carried out in an efficient manner.”1  PJM 
Interconnection, L.L.C.’s (“PJM”) current stakeholder process falls short of this principle.  
Chairman Laura Swett summarized the PJM stakeholder process recently as “slow where it must 
be fast, opaque where it must be transparent, and vulnerable to vetoes and agenda control exactly 
when the region needs immediate action.”2  Chairman Swett’s observation aptly sets forth three 
priorities the Commission should seek to bolster through PJM governance reforms: efficiency, 
transparency, and independence. 
 
1  
Promoting Wholesale Competition Through Open Access Non-discriminatory Transmission Services by Public 
Utilities and Recovery of Stranded Costs by Public Utilities and Transmitting Utilities, Order No. 888, 61 Fed. 
Reg. 21,540 (May 10, 1996) FERC Stats. & Regs. ¶ 31,036 (1996) (providing 11 principles that FERC would use 
in evaluating the creation of voluntary ISOs, including: (1) the ISO’s governance should be fair and non-
discriminatory; (2) the ISO and its employees must have no financial interest in the performance of any power 
market participant; (3) the ISO should provide open access; (4) the ISO is primarily responsible for short-term 
reliability; (5) the ISO must have control over the interconnection of transmission; (6) the ISO should be able to 
identify and relieve constraints on its system; (7) the ISO should have appropriate incentives for efficient 
management and administration and management and administration of the ISO should be carried out in an 
efficient manner; (8) the ISO’s pricing policies should promote efficient use and investment in generation, 
transmission, and consumption; (9) transmission system information should be publicly available on a timely 
basis; (10) the ISO should develop mechanism to coordinate with neighboring areas; and (11) alternative dispute 
resolution procedures should be established as a first resort to dispute resolution within the ISO). 
2  
Chairman Laura Swett’s Comments at PJM’s Annual Meeting in Baltimore, MD (May 12, 2026), at 
https://www.ferc.gov/news-events/news/chairman-laura-swetts-comments-pjms-annual-meeting-baltimore-md-
0.

2 
 
Talen Energy Corporation (“Talen”) welcomes the opportunity presented by the 
Commission to comment on PJM’s governance and stakeholder process.  Talen also encourages 
the Commission to use every tool it possesses to further reforms that will result in PJM’s increased 
efficiency and transparency, while protecting the independence of the PJM Board. 
I. 
MOTION TO INTERVENE 
Pursuant to Rule 214 of the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure,3 Talen 
respectfully submits this motion to intervene in the above-captioned proceeding.  The formal legal 
name of Talen is Talen Energy Corporation.  Talen is a corporation organized and existing under 
the laws of Delaware.  Talen maintains its principal place of business at 2929 Allen Parkway, 22nd 
Floor, Houston, Texas 77019. Talen is a leading independent power producer and energy 
infrastructure company which owns and operates approximately 15.7 gigawatts of power 
infrastructure in the United States.  Talen produces and sells electricity, capacity, and ancillary 
services into wholesale U.S. power markets, including and primarily in PJM.  Accordingly, the 
actions taken by the Commission in this matter will directly affect the interests of Talen.  Talen 
has a direct and material interest in the instant proceeding that no other party can adequately 
represent.  Talen therefore requests that the Commission grant this motion to intervene and permit 
Talen to participate in this proceeding with full rights as a party thereto. 
II. 
COMMENTS    
The Federal Power Act (“FPA”) provides the Commission with authority to regulate ISOs 
and regional transmission organizations (“RTOs”), such as PJM, as “public utilities” because the 
 
3  
18 C.F.R. § 385.214 (2026).

3 
 
RTOs operate the interstate transmission system.4  As a result, FERC has jurisdiction under FPA 
Sections 205 and 206 over PJM’s stakeholder process because the stakeholder process “provides 
input that directly affects the content of jurisdictional practices” and “is one that directly affects 
jurisdictional rates.”5  The Commission should not hesitate to exercise its jurisdiction to improve 
the governance and stakeholder process of the largest energy market in the country and ensure that 
the RTO, including its Board, remains compliant with the Commission’s RTO principles set forth 
in Order No. 888 and Order No. 2000.6    
A. 
Talen supports reforms that would result in increased efficiency in the PJM 
stakeholder and decision-making process.  
Electric sector innovation will not wait for PJM.  Rather, PJM must meet the moment.  
There may be instances where imminent and significant decisions must be made quickly to keep 
pace with the industry or reliability considerations.  PJM’s existing stakeholder process has proven 
inadequate in this regard.  For example, recent and significant Critical Issue Fast Path (“CIFP”) 
proceedings proved unproductive.  PJM’s 2026 CIFP combining Reliability Backstop 
Procurement (RBP) and the Connect & Manage (C&M) put forth about a dozen proposals for each 
 
4  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 101 FERC ¶ 61,318 at P 25 (2002) (explaining that PJM “as the operator of the 
transmission facilities that make up the PJM grid and the provider of transmission services within the PJM control 
area, is just as much a public utility as the owners of those facilities”). 
5  
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., 157 FERC ¶ 61,229 at P 11 (2016); FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 
260, 278 (2016) (providing that FERC’s jurisdiction under FPA Sections 205 and 206 are limited to practices that 
“directly affect the [wholesale rate]”); see also New England Power Pool Participants Committee, 166 FERC ¶ 
61,062 at P 48 (2019) (holding that the New England Power Pool Participants Committee “rules with respect to 
membership fall within the Commission’s jurisdiction because they directly affect Commission-jurisdictional 
rates”). 
6  
Supra at n.1; Order No. 2000, Regional Transmission Organizations, 89 FERC ¶ 61,285 at p. 38 (1999) (providing 
that RTO independence is based on three main criteria: (1) RTO employes and directors have no financial stake 
in any market participant; (2) the RTO must have a decision-making process that is independent of control by any 
market participant or class of participants; and (3) the RTO must have exclusive and independent authority to file 
changes to its transmission tariff).

4 
 
issue, with only one RBP proposal receiving stakeholder support.7  The CFIP process for Large 
Load Additions in 2025 required months of member-driven deliberations and led to twelve 
separate proposals, none of which were approved by the required threshold of votes.8  In addition, 
the 2023 CIFP on resource adequacy resulted in 20 rejected packages.9  PJM should avoid such 
quagmires for certain issues that the PJM Board deems a priority.  PJM could publish such priority 
issues annually, with quarterly updates or on an individual, one-off basis as determined by the PJM 
Board in its discretion.  For an issue that has previously been subject to the stakeholder deliberation 
process but has lagged therein for any reason, then, to the extent that the PJM Board believes it 
must act unilaterally, the Board should also be able to label such issues as a priority to avoid further 
undue delay. 
For imminent, priority concerns, the stakeholder process should become advisory.  That 
does not mean the stakeholder process would be circumvented altogether.  The PJM Board can 
benefit from the insights, expertise, and opinions of stakeholders; however, the Board should be 
able to move quickly to address imminent issues without the need for a prolonged stakeholder 
process. Similar advisory processes have already been adopted by the California Independent 
 
7  
Leith-Yessian, Devin, PJM Stakeholders Endorse 1 Backstop Procurement Proposal, Reject ‘Connect and 
Manage’, RTO INSIDER (June 30, 2026), available at https://www.rtoinsider.com/135656-pjm-stakeholders-
endorse-backstop-procurement-proposal-reject-connect-and-manage/. 
8  
Leith-Yessian, Devin, PJM Stakeholders Reject all CIFP Proposals on Large Loads, RTO INSIDER (Nov. 20, 
2025), available at https://www.rtoinsider.com/120206-pjm-stakeholders-reject-all-cifp-proposals-large-loads/. 
9  
Leith-Yessian, Devin, PJM Pushing Forward on Efforts to Meet Rising Data Center Load, RTO INSIDER (Jan. 5, 
2026), available at https://www.rtoinsider.com/122643-pjm-pushing-forward-on-efforts-to-meet-rising-data-
center-load/.

5 
 
System Operator (“CAISO”),10 the Midcontinent Independent System Operator (“MISO”)11 and 
the Southwest Power Pool (“SPP”).12  Consequently, PJM should have FPA Section 205 filing 
rights unencumbered by the requirement to obtain approval of two-thirds of the Members 
Committee for issues the Board has deemed a priority.  This can extend to issues involving the 
energy market, ancillary services, regional transmission expansion planning, etc.  There is no need 
to lower the Members Committee approval threshold from two-thirds sector-weighted voting for 
issues not deemed a priority. 
If member votes become advisory for deemed priority issues, then it is reasonable for the 
Members Committee to have recourse in the form of “jump ball” filing rights over portions of the 
PJM Tariff when a supermajority of stakeholders approves an alternative proposal.  Such a right 
would be consistent with the ISO New England’s process, whereby the New England Power Pool 
(“NEPOOL”) may file an alternative proposal under FPA Section 205 if 60% or more stakeholders 
are in support.13  However, FERC and PJM should cooperate to determine the best way to enable 
stakeholders to independently reach consensus similar to the dedicated stakeholder process 
administered by NEPOOL.  Subject to the limitations and context above, Talen votes “yes” on 
Nos. 11, 12, 13, and 15, and votes “no” on No. 16. 
 
10  Corporate Governance Principles, Version #4.2, CALIFORNIA INDEPENDENT SYSTEM OPERATOR (Oct. 15, 2025) 
(establishing that the CAISO board shall consider stakeholder input, but will ultimately hold decision-making 
authority).  
11  Agreement of Transmission Facilities Owners to Organize the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc., 
MIDCONTINENT INDEPENDENT SYSTEM OPERATOR, INC. (affirming that the MISO Advisory Committee will not 
excersie control over the MISO board or MISO). 
12  Governing Documents Tariff, SOUTHWEST POWER POOL (March 31, 2026) (establishing SPP stakeholder 
committees as “advisory” committees). 
13  Participants Agreement among ISO New England Inc. and the New England Power Pool and the Individual 
Participants § 11.1.5.

6 
 
PJM States should also have a role in the stakeholder process. Talen generally supports 
State involvement because States have a unique perspective to be able to opine on local issues and 
priorities.  For this reason, Talen is supportive of providing a second state representative group 
consisting of governors’ representatives and/or state legislators’ representatives, in addition to the 
Organization of PJM States Inc. (“OPSI”). 
Talen also supports OPSI consultation early in the stakeholder process.  It would arguably 
be too late and inefficient to consult with OPSI “prior to making a section 205 filing” because any 
constructive feedback from OPSI would need to be circulated through the stakeholders again.   
Talen further supports allowing states to vote for informational purposes on motions before 
the Members Committee.  However, providing formal voting rights to States puts PJM on the 
precipice of a slippery slope.  The Federal Power Act provides the Commission with exclusive 
jurisdiction over wholesale sales of electricity in the interstate market and “leaves to the States 
alone, the regulation of [retail electricity sales.]14  States cannot set an interstate wholesale rate 
because it would “contraven[e] the FPA’s division of authority between state and federal 
regulators.”15  Accordingly, providing States formal voting rights—or providing OPSI “jump ball” 
filing rights—is ill-conceived and arguably inconsistent with the FPA.  States and state 
commissions may continue to initiate their own proceedings with FERC should they desire to do 
so.16  Subject to the limitations and context above, Talen votes “yes” on Nos. 9, 18, and 20 
and votes “no” on Nos. 14 and 19. 
 
14  FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 264 (2016).  
15  Hughes v. Talen Energy Marketing, LLC, 578 U.S. 150, 163 (2016).  
16  See, e.g., 18 C.F.R. § 385.206 (providing that any organization or person can file a complaint against another 
party alleging violation of a statute, rule, order, or other law administered by FERC or any other alleged wrong 
over which FERC may have jurisdiction).

7 
 
B. 
Talen supports reforms that would result in increased transparency in the 
PJM stakeholder and decision-making process. 
Reasoned decision-making ensures that there is a logical corollary between the facts 
presented and the decision made.  Further, reasoned decision-making protects the legitimacy of 
the decision-maker.17  The PJM Board should provide the vote count and a reasoned explanation 
(similar to Decisional Letters) based on the facts and issues considered that resulted in the decision 
rendered.  For this reason, Talen votes “yes” on No. 6. 
Legitimacy is also fostered when voting rules bar the furtherance of affiliate interests.  As 
such, Talen also supports applying voting rules barring affiliate votes to lower-level committees.  
For this reason, Talen votes “yes” on No. 17. 
Notwithstanding the need for increased transparency, some existing and proposed 
measures may be counterproductive towards the goal of increased efficiency.  For example, 
restrictions on Board and stakeholder communications may undermine efforts to coalesce around 
best paths forward for imminent or priority issues.  More frequent and recurring meetings between 
the Board and stakeholders would be beneficial for all parties. The Board should also be permitted 
to entertain individual meeting requests for imminent or “priority” issues.  Subject to this 
limitation and context, Talen votes “yes” on No. 5. 
In addition, opening Board meetings to the public may unnecessarily politicize the Board’s 
decisions and delay progress.  PJM would not be alone in holding closed Board meetings.18  For 
 
17  Cf., supra at n.2 (Chairman Swett explaining that complaints regarding PJM’s stakeholder process “are warning 
signs of a serious legitimacy crisis and a signal that confidence in PJM’s decision making has completely 
eroded”). 
18  See ISO-NE, By-Laws, Art. IV (Board meetings are only open to the directors and ISO-NE management); By-
Laws of the New York Independent System Operating, Inc., Art. III, sec. 1(c) (Board meetings are closed to 
Stakeholders, though representatives from FERC and the NYPSC may attend as non-voting participants).

8 
 
this reason, Talen votes “no” on No. 7.  If public guests are allowed in Board meetings, they 
should be pre-registered, at the invitation of a member, and appear in-person.   
C. 
Talen supports reforms that would protect the independence of the PJM 
Board. 
The Commission explained in Order No. 2000, that RTO independence is based on three 
main criteria: (1) RTO employes and directors have no financial stake in any market participant; 
(2) the RTO must have a decision-making process that is independent of control by any market 
participant or class of participants; and (3) the RTO must have exclusive and independent authority 
to file changes to its transmission tariff.19  The Commission should ensure PJM’s compliance with 
this criteria, but additional restrictions that becomes superfluous or restrict PJM’s ability to attract 
the best talent to serve on its Board are unnecessary.  For example, Board member qualification 
rules should not include a preference for PJM residents.  Prior experience with and an aptitude for 
PJM issues is more important than PJM residence.  In addition, “cooling off” periods with respect 
to conflict-of-interest rules are unnecessary, provided that all financial conflict of interest rules 
remain intact and consistent with Order No. 2000. This approach would be consistent with how 
other ISO/RTOs, such as CAISO,20 the Electric Reliability Council of Texas,21 the Independent 
System Operator of New England,22 the New York Independent System Operator (“NYISO”)23 
 
19  Supra at n.7. 
20  See CA Public Utilities Code § 337(b); and Board Selection Policy, Version #5.5, CALIFORNIA INDEPENDENT 
SYSTEM OPERATOR (Oct. 19, 2025).    
21  See Amended and Restated Bylaws of Electric Reliability Council of Texas, Inc., ELECTRIC RELIABILITY COUNCIL 
OF TEXAS, INC. (approved on Dec. 20, 2022); and ERCOT Code of Conduct – The Way We Work, ELECTRIC 
RELIABILITY COUNCIL OF TEXAS, INC.   
22  See Participants Agreement among ISO New England Inc. and the New England Power Pool and the Individual 
Participants; and ISO New England Inc. Code of Conduct. 
23  See By-Laws of the New York Independent System Operator, Inc.

9 
 
and SPP,24 rely on financial conflict of interest rules instead of using a “cooling off” period.25  
Accordingly, Talen votes “no” on No. 3 and votes “yes” on No. 4. 
It is also not advisable to revise PJM’s governing documents in a manner that could subvert 
the Board’s independence.  Tying management compensation to the achievement of public 
performance metrics is one such example.  The Board is often called on to make difficult decisions 
that are in the best interests of stakeholders and the public in the long term.  A perverse incentive 
could be created if a Board member’s compensation was tied to short-term metrics.  For this 
reason, Talen votes “no” on No. 10.   
It is also unnecessary to include a “public interest” responsibility in PJM’s governing 
documents.  Section 7.7(i) of PJM’s Operating Agreement already provides that the Board’s 
Primary responsibility” is to  
ensure that the President, the other officers of the LLC, and Office 
of the Interconnection perform the duties and responsibilities set 
forth in the Agreement, including . . . the safe and reliable operation 
of the PJM Region . . . operation of a robust, competitive, and non-
discriminatory electric power market in the PJM Region, and . . . 
shall not have undue influence over the operation of the PJM 
Region.26  
As a result, including a “public interest” responsibility would be redundant at best.27    For this 
reason, Talen votes “no” on No. 8. 
 
24  Governing Documents Tariff, SOUTHWEST POWER POOL (March 31, 2026).  
25  MISO similarly reduced its cooling off period from two years to one year in 2017. See Midcontinent Independent 
System Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER17-686-000 (delegated letter order) (issued on Feb. 23, 2017).  
26  PJM Operating Agreement at Section 7.7(i) (Duties and Responsibilities of the PJM Board) (emphasis added). 
27  The only RTO/ISO with a specific “public interest” principle is CAISO and the principle is established by the 
Public Utility Code.  See Ca. Pub. Utility Code § 345.5(a) (providing that CAISO “shall conduct its operations 
consistent with applicable state and federal laws and consistent with the interests of the people of the state”).

10 
 
Independence can also be reinforced by longer terms, subject to overall caps.  Further, 
Board members should have staggered terms, with 3 seats expiring each cycle allowing for a full 
Board turnover every 6-years.  Talen supports a 6-year term, with a 2-term limit (for a total of 12 
years).  The twelve-year total term limit is consistent with NYISO’s practice.28  Board members’ 
terms should expire every 2 years on a staggered basis, to preserve continuity and stability on the 
Board.  Subject to this limitation and context, Talen votes “yes” on Nos. 1 and 2. 
 
28  NYISO Bylaws at Art. II, Sec. 4 and Art. III, Sec. 3(b).

III. 
CONCLUSION  
Talen appreciates the opportunity to opine on the PJM governance and stakeholder process.  
The issues facing the RTO are too important and pressing to be bogged down by the existing 
stakeholder process.  The Commission has identified certain measures that would increase the 
efficiency and transparency of PJM, while protecting the independence of the PJM Board.  Talen 
respectfully requests that the Commission consider its comments provided herein.  For ease of 
reference, Talen has attached hereto an Appendix with its standalone answers to the Commission’s 
questions.
